多姆貝克鼓以單面膜鳴發聲，輕擊時共鳴明顯而餘音短。中央以指掌打出低沉開放音，邊緣: The doumbek sounds with a single head. Struck lightly it resonates clearly but the sound dies quickly. In the centre the fingers and palm produce a low, open tone, and at the edge the fingertips produce a higher note; pressing the palm on the head damps it, and moving a fist in and out of the opening changes the timbre. The Egyptian rounded rim favours fast rolls, while the Turkish exposed rim makes finger snaps easier but fast rolls harder; compared with West African hand drums the touch is lighter and the fingering different.
多姆貝克鼓常見於北非、中東與巴爾幹傳統音樂，亦見於南亞、東歐傳統音樂；蘇拉威西的: The doumbek is common in the traditional music of North Africa, the Middle East and the Balkans, and also in that of South Asia and eastern Europe; the large goblet drums of Sulawesi serve as temple instruments. In Western classical music, the Dance of the Nubian Slaves in Act IV of Berlioz's opera Les Troyens calls for a tarbuka; Halim El-Dabh wrote for goblet drum and orchestra, and his Fantasia-Tahmeel, for goblet drum and strings, was premiered in New York in 1958 with Stokowski conducting the strings.
多姆貝克鼓（Doumbek）是單面膜鳴鼓，H-S 211.26，鼓身呈杯形。它常: The doumbek is a single-headed membranophone, H-S 211.26, with a goblet-shaped body. It is common in the traditional music of North Africa, the Middle East and the Balkans and also in South Asia and eastern Europe; the large goblet drums of Sulawesi serve as temple instruments and are placed on the ground. Players usually tuck the drum under the arm or lay it on its side on the knee and strike it with the fingertips and palm; some drums have a strap so that they can be used standing or while dancing.
杯鼓為單面膜鳴樂器，發聲分類211.26，存在數千年，曾見於美索不達米亞、古埃及: The goblet drum is a single-headed membranophone, sounding classification 211.26, and has existed for thousands of years; it is found in Mesopotamia, ancient Egypt, Babylon and Sumer, and can be traced back to 1100 BC. It was later widely used in the traditional music of North Africa, the Middle East and the Balkans and appears in South Asia and eastern Europe; the large goblet drums of Sulawesi, set on the ground as temple instruments, may reflect an ancient use. The name darbuka comes from Egyptian rural Arabic, from darb, to strike. In 1856 to 1858 Berlioz's opera Les Troyens used a tarbuka; in the 1950s Halim El-Dabh wrote for goblet drum and orchestra, and in 1958 his Fantasia-Tahmeel was premiered in New York with Stokowski conducting.
演奏時可夾於腋下或置於腿上，鼓面朝膝；初學先以指尖與掌輕擊，中央出低音，邊緣出高: Play it tucked under the arm or resting on the leg with the head facing the knee. A beginner should strike lightly with the fingertips and palm: the centre gives the low note, the edge the high one, and the off hand's high note is the fill note; laying the palm on the head closes the sound. The Egyptian rounded rim favours fast rolls, and the Turkish exposed rim allows finger snaps. You can also use the fingers of one hand and a thin stick in the other.
